text: Background: Pedestrians are exposed to highly localised acoustic environments that are poorly represented by conventional monitoring stations or coarse noise maps, which is especially important when considering continuous soundscape monitoring of pedestrian streets. Sound conditions vary sharply over short distances but are usually characterised by sparse measurement. The investigation evaluated a sensing-based workflow for continuous soundscape monitoring of pedestrian streets without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. Methods: A network of calibrated acoustic nodes was installed along pedestrian streets and recorded equivalent and percentile sound levels continuously for eight months. Spectral descriptors were computed and clustered to distinguish traffic-dominated from activity-dominated soundscapes. After preprocessing, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. To preserve the practical meaning of continuous soundscape monitoring of pedestrian streets, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. Results: The resulting measurements were contrasted in relation to observed differences in pedestrian use, comfort or accessibility where such data were available to identify locations at which coarse neighbourhood measures would conceal important differences. Segments classified as activity-dominated coincided with locations exhibiting higher observed pedestrian dwell time. Conclusions: At network scale, these findings indicate that acoustic quality can be represented as a spatially explicit component of pedestrian environmental assessment rather than treated only as a citywide noise indicator, with particular relevance to continuous soundscape monitoring of pedestrian streets.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Children walking to school may experience elevated pollutant exposure. Regulatory air-quality stations provide useful regional information but do not describe the concentrations encountered by pedestrians at street level, which is especially important when considering monitoring pedestrian-level air quality along school routes. The analysis tested a sensing-based workflow for monitoring pedestrian-level air quality along school routes without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. Calibrated low-cost nitrogen dioxide and particulate sensors were installed at pedestrian height along designated school routes and co-located with a reference monitor for calibration. Hourly concentrations were mapped and compared between route alternatives. After preprocessing, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level to avoid masking local differences through area-wide averaging. Interior street alternatives showed consistently lower concentrations, and the measured differentials informed revision of recommended school route designations. The processed observations were compared across contrasting route types and local environmental contexts to identify locations at which coarse neighbourhood measures would conceal important differences. Before interpreting monitoring pedestrian-level air quality along school routes, the authors screened the measurements for missing values, implausible readings and periods of incomplete spatial coverage. Some short-term variability remained after preprocessing, although it was smaller than the persistent differences observed between route segments when interpreting results for monitoring pedestrian-level air quality along school routes. Taken together, the study demonstrates the value of incorporating measured pollutant exposure into assessments of the healthfulness and comfort of walking routes, while retaining the local detail needed for interpreting monitoring pedestrian-level air quality along school routes.

text: Systematic characterisation of microclimate along pedestrian routes requires dense spatial sampling. Microclimatic conditions can change within tens of metres, making neighbourhood-average temperature a poor proxy for the thermal environment experienced during walking, creating a methodological challenge for studies of thermal comfort mapping of pedestrian networks using bicycle-mounted mobile sensing. This work investigated a reproducible approach to thermal comfort mapping of pedestrian networks using bicycle-mounted mobile sensing under real-world conditions. A bicycle-mounted instrument package recorded air temperature, humidity, wind speed and mean radiant temperature along repeated transects covering the pedestrian network of a mid-sized city. Data were corrected for sensor response time and aggregated by street segment. For spatial analysis, measurements were time-stamped and linked to individual walking segments while keeping the component measure interpretable for later walkability analysis. Derived comfort indices identified a consistent set of thermally disadvantaged corridors linking residential areas to transit. The route-level indicators were contrasted in relation to observed differences in pedestrian use, comfort or accessibility where such data were available to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. To preserve the practical meaning of thermal comfort mapping of pedestrian networks using bicycle-mounted mobile sensing, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. Coverage was constrained by the acquisition design, but repeated observations suggested that the main spatial pattern was not driven by a single survey period before generalising findings about thermal comfort mapping of pedestrian networks using bicycle-mounted mobile sensing. In practical terms, the results support the use of pedestrian-scale thermal measurements when prioritising shade, material or route interventions under hot-weather conditions, providing a practical basis for future work on thermal comfort mapping of pedestrian networks using bicycle-mounted mobile sensing.

text: The study evaluated whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for structured light scanning of tactile paving continuity on urban footways while preserving variation between adjacent walking segments. Small geometric discontinuities in pedestrian infrastructure can determine whether a route is usable, yet they are rarely documented consistently across an urban network, a concern directly relevant to structured light scanning of tactile paving continuity on urban footways. Tactile surfaces guide visually impaired pedestrians but degrade and are frequently interrupted by works. Handheld structured light scanning captured the geometry of tactile paving along designated guidance routes, from which profile height, spacing and continuity breaks were extracted. Automated detection of interruptions was validated against manual inspection. Once the observations had been screened, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated while keeping the component measure interpretable for later walkability analysis. The route-level indicators were examined in relation to observed differences in pedestrian use, comfort or accessibility where such data were available to identify locations at which coarse neighbourhood measures would conceal important differences. More than a fifth of the guidance network contained breaks exceeding the length considered navigable. For structured light scanning of tactile paving continuity on urban footways, reference observations were kept separate from the main processing wherever possible so that agreement could be evaluated independently. Overall, the approach demonstrates how three-dimensional sensing can support consistent pedestrian-infrastructure assessment at network scale, with particular relevance to structured light scanning of tactile paving continuity on urban footways.

text: Assessing a walking network requires information about the quality and operation of crossings rather than simply their location, which is especially important when considering fixed camera observation of pedestrian crossing behaviour and infrastructure adequacy. Crossing provision can be evaluated by observing how it is actually used. The investigation investigated a sensing-based workflow for fixed camera observation of pedestrian crossing behaviour and infrastructure adequacy without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. Fixed cameras recorded pedestrian crossing movements at twelve intersections, and an automated tracking pipeline extracted crossing trajectories, waiting times and non-compliant crossings. Observed behaviour was related to measured crossing geometry and signal timing. Following quality control, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. To preserve the practical meaning of fixed camera observation of pedestrian crossing behaviour and infrastructure adequacy, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. The resulting measurements were compared across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to evaluate the extent to which the measure represented a distinct dimension of the walking environment. Intersections with longer crossing distances and shorter clearance intervals exhibited higher rates of incomplete crossings. At network scale, the findings provide direct evidence for identifying crossings where infrastructure or operation interrupts otherwise continuous pedestrian routes, while retaining the local detail needed for interpreting fixed camera observation of pedestrian crossing behaviour and infrastructure adequacy.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Distance alone is an incomplete measure of pedestrian accessibility when route geometry and physical barriers vary substantially, a concern directly relevant to auditing sidewalk accessibility barriers. Manual accessibility audits are difficult to scale. This work tested a reproducible approach to auditing sidewalk accessibility barriers so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. A pedestrian-borne camera with GNSS logging captured continuous video along the footway network, and a detection model identified barriers including steps, poles, temporary signage and surface breaks. Detections were georeferenced and aggregated to segments. Following quality control, the retained observations were georeferenced and attached to the pedestrian network so that short-distance variation remained visible. Because auditing sidewalk accessibility barriers may vary both spatially and temporally, the two sources of variation were examined separately before producing route-level summaries. The segment-level estimates were analysed across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. Agreement with expert manual audit reached substantial levels, and the resulting barrier map supported prioritisation of remediation works. In practical terms, the resulting route-level attributes can support accessibility analysis that reflects physical effort and barriers rather than relying on distance alone, with particular relevance to auditing sidewalk accessibility barriers.

text: The investigation evaluated a sensing-based workflow for pedestrian solar exposure assessment without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score with attention to repeatability and measurement validity. Microclimatic conditions can change within tens of metres, making neighbourhood-average temperature a poor proxy for the thermal environment experienced during walking, creating a methodological challenge for studies of pedestrian solar exposure assessment. Solar access at pedestrian level governs both summer discomfort and winter usability. Fisheye images were captured at pedestrian height at a systematic sample of points and processed to compute sky view factor and directional solar obstruction. Values were validated against measurements derived from surveyed building geometry. For spatial analysis, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level while keeping the component measure interpretable for later walkability analysis. The spatial outputs were interpreted between neighbouring links with otherwise similar network characteristics to identify locations at which coarse neighbourhood measures would conceal important differences. The resulting maps identified street orientations where summer exposure and winter shading simultaneously reach unfavourable values. Overall, these observations show that thermal comfort is sufficiently localised to warrant direct inclusion in fine-grained walkability assessment, while retaining the local detail needed for interpreting pedestrian solar exposure assessment.

text: The study examined a sensing-based workflow for multi-sensor assessment of walking environments at a transport interchange without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score under real-world conditions. Recent sensing and computational approaches provide new opportunities to measure components of the walking environment directly rather than infer them from coarse proxies, creating a methodological challenge for studies of multi-sensor assessment of walking environments at a transport interchange. Automated characterisation of walking conditions can reduce reliance on surveys. A wearable system combining inertial sensors, barometric altimetry and a forward-facing camera was used to classify walking environments encountered at a transport interchange, distinguishing level surfaces, ramps, stairs and uneven paving. In the final processing stage, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. The spatial outputs were interpreted between neighbouring links with otherwise similar network characteristics to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. Several classifiers were compared and the best configuration exceeded 90 percent accuracy against annotated ground truth, enabling automated profiling of access routes. Because multi-sensor assessment of walking environments at a transport interchange may vary both spatially and temporally, the two sources of variation were examined separately before producing route-level summaries. The authors note that transfer to other cities will depend on local morphology, sensor placement and the availability of comparable reference data for applications involving multi-sensor assessment of walking environments at a transport interchange. In practical terms, the study provides a repeatable method for adding fine-grained environmental evidence to pedestrian network assessment and intervention planning, providing a practical basis for future work on multi-sensor assessment of walking environments at a transport interchange.

text: Conventional inventories typically record the nominal presence of sidewalks or crossings but omit the fine-scale geometry that governs accessibility; the present study addressed this issue through vegetation encroachment on footways from mobile imagery and range data. The research tested a sensing-based workflow for vegetation encroachment on footways from mobile imagery and range data without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score at a resolution suitable for pedestrian-environment assessment. Overgrown vegetation reduces effective walking width and forces pedestrians onto the carriageway. Mobile mapping imagery and lidar returns were processed to detect vegetation intruding into the pedestrian clearance envelope, quantifying intrusion depth and height. Detections were compared with maintenance complaint records. After preprocessing, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. The processed observations were analysed against relevant guidance thresholds and complementary streetscape variables to separate persistent environmental differences from short-term fluctuations. Automated detection identified substantially more encroachment locations than the complaint-driven process, most of them on low-traffic residential streets. Before interpreting vegetation encroachment on footways from mobile imagery and range data, the authors screened the measurements for missing values, implausible readings and periods of incomplete spatial coverage. Taken together, the approach demonstrates how three-dimensional sensing can support consistent pedestrian-infrastructure assessment at network scale, providing a practical basis for future work on vegetation encroachment on footways from mobile imagery and range data.

text: Background: Pedestrian lighting is often evaluated from asset records even though delivered light levels can vary markedly along the same street, creating a methodological challenge for studies of illuminance and luminance mapping of pedestrian underpasses using calibrated imaging. Underpasses concentrate perceived insecurity within pedestrian networks. The investigation examined whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for illuminance and luminance mapping of pedestrian underpasses using calibrated imaging under real-world conditions. Methods: Calibrated luminance imaging and point illuminance measurement were carried out in fourteen underpasses at night, producing spatial distributions of light level, uniformity and glare. Measured metrics were compared against design guidance and against user ratings collected on site. Following quality control, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. For illuminance and luminance mapping of pedestrian underpasses using calibrated imaging, reference observations were kept separate from the main processing wherever possible so that agreement could be evaluated independently. Results: The segment-level estimates were interpreted across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to separate persistent environmental differences from short-term fluctuations. Uniformity, rather than mean illuminance, showed the strongest association with reported reassurance. Conclusions: At network scale, the findings support route-level lighting assessment as part of evaluating the usability and reassurance of pedestrian networks after dark, with particular relevance to illuminance and luminance mapping of pedestrian underpasses using calibrated imaging.

text: Continuous pedestrian counts support evaluation of streetscape investment. Pedestrian crossings can create substantial delay or difficulty even when they are formally present in municipal inventories, creating a methodological challenge for studies of pedestrian volume estimation from wireless signal detection on commercial streets. The investigation investigated whether pedestrian volume estimation from wireless signal detection on commercial streets could be characterised consistently at pedestrian scale with attention to repeatability and measurement validity. Wireless probe request detection was deployed on commercial streets, with detection rates calibrated against synchronised manual counts and correction factors estimated for device carriage rates. Continuous volume estimates were produced for eighteen months spanning a public realm improvement. In the final processing stage, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated so that short-distance variation remained visible. Post-intervention volumes rose significantly relative to comparison streets after controlling for weather and seasonality. The processed observations were analysed across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to assess whether the observed pattern was sufficiently stable for practical interpretation. Taken together, the findings provide direct evidence for identifying crossings where infrastructure or operation interrupts otherwise continuous pedestrian routes, providing a practical basis for future work on pedestrian volume estimation from wireless signal detection on commercial streets.

text: Pedestrians are exposed to highly localised acoustic environments that are poorly represented by conventional monitoring stations or coarse noise maps, a concern directly relevant to comprehensive footway assessment. The analysis tested a sensing-based workflow for comprehensive footway assessment without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score with attention to repeatability and measurement validity. Image-based assessment scales well but cannot capture non-visual attributes. This study paired citywide segmentation of street imagery, yielding sidewalk presence, width and greenery, with stratified field measurement of surface roughness, illuminance and sound level at 300 sampled segments. A statistical model transferred the field-measured attributes to unmeasured segments using visual predictors. In the final processing stage, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level so that short-distance variation remained visible. The resulting measurements were contrasted across contrasting route types and local environmental contexts to determine whether the sensed attribute captured meaningful local variation. Cross-validation indicated acceptable transfer accuracy for illuminance and roughness but not for sound level. To preserve the practical meaning of comprehensive footway assessment, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. The measured attribute represents only one component of walkability and should be interpreted alongside complementary accessibility, safety and comfort indicators before generalising findings about comprehensive footway assessment. From a pedestrian-planning perspective, the approach provides route-level evidence that can complement visual and geometric measures of walkability when comfort and restorative quality are considered, providing a practical basis for future work on comprehensive footway assessment.

text: Diversity of land use is a recognised correlate of travel behaviour. Composite walkability indices are widely used to compare neighbourhoods and investigate associations with travel or health outcomes; the present study addressed this issue through land use mix and transport mode share in medium-sized european cities. The analysis modelled associations relevant to land use mix and transport mode share in medium-sized european cities at the spatial and temporal scale required by that application. This study computes entropy-based land use mix indicators from cadastral records for medium-sized cities and relates them to mode share reported in national travel surveys. Multilevel models control for household characteristics and city size. Following data harmonisation, the observations were divided into calibration and evaluation subsets with sensitivity analyses used to test the stability of the main result. Land use mix showed a positive association with walking mode share, though the magnitude varied considerably between national contexts. The estimated associations were compared with attention to the variables contributing most strongly to the primary outcome to assess robustness and practical relevance. For land use mix and transport mode share in medium-sized european cities, the authors reported both overall performance and context-specific variation rather than relying on a single average estimate. Performance varied across subgroups or spatial contexts, indicating that recalibration may be required before transfer to other settings when interpreting results for land use mix and transport mode share in medium-sized european cities. In practical terms, the study contributes to the construction and interpretation of area-based walkability measures from routinely available spatial data, while keeping the interpretation centred on land use mix and transport mode share in medium-sized european cities.

text: The research modelled how the available urban or sensor-derived variables contributed to machine learning prediction of street tree failure risk with calibration and validation tailored to the target outcome. Automated extraction of streetscape features is becoming common across several domains of urban analytics; the present study addressed this issue through machine learning prediction of street tree failure risk. Tree failure poses risks to property and people in cities. This study applied regression trees and ensemble methods to predict failure using attributes obtainable in routine field inspection, including species, diameter, surrounding building height and district age. Models were trained on municipal failure records over a decade. After preprocessing, the principal explanatory variables were entered into the statistical or machine-learning model with sensitivity analyses used to test the stability of the main result. The evaluation metrics were contrasted across spatial contexts relevant to the target application to assess robustness and practical relevance. Surrounding building height and district age emerged as the dominant predictors, supporting risk-based scheduling of preventive maintenance. For the analysis of machine learning prediction of street tree failure risk, reference observations were kept separate from model fitting wherever possible so that reported performance reflected out-of-sample behaviour. In practical terms, the approach is intended to improve prediction or management of the target urban outcome at fine spatial resolution, supporting the study's primary application involving machine learning prediction of street tree failure risk.

text: Immersive environments offer controlled presentation of design alternatives. Simulation provides a controlled framework for testing how design alternatives may influence environmental conditions or pedestrian behaviour before physical intervention, which is especially important when considering streetscape preference elicitation. This work modelled the performance of the proposed approach for streetscape preference elicitation with calibration and validation tailored to the target outcome. Participants viewed reconstructed street scenes in a head-mounted display and rated preference and perceived quality across systematically varied design parameters. Ratings were analysed with mixed models. After preprocessing, the available variables were aligned to the spatial unit required by the target analysis while retaining the outcome definition used in the source application. The protocol produced consistent preference orderings, and its reliability relative to photographic presentation is discussed; no measurement of existing physical environments was undertaken. The evaluation metrics were examined against domain-specific reference data and baseline methods to assess robustness and practical relevance. For streetscape preference elicitation, the authors reported both overall performance and context-specific variation rather than relying on a single average estimate. From an implementation perspective, the model provides a framework for comparing design scenarios and testing the sensitivity of predicted outcomes to alternative assumptions, with the principal contribution remaining the analysis of streetscape preference elicitation.

text: The investigation modelled household travel survey analysis of walking trip generation in relation to the study's primary outcome at the spatial and temporal scale required by that application. Digital urban data support analyses ranging from infrastructure management to travel demand, public health and behavioural modelling, creating a methodological challenge for studies of household travel survey analysis of walking trip generation. Trip generation models underpin transport demand forecasting. This study analyses walking trip rates reported in a metropolitan household travel survey, disaggregated by household composition, income and residential location type. Count models were estimated and compared. In the modelling stage, the data sources were harmonised before estimation of the study's primary outcome with robustness checked under alternative specifications. The predictive results were examined across alternative specifications and study subgroups to assess robustness and practical relevance. Results indicate systematic underreporting of short walking stages and propose correction factors derived from a supplementary diary validation exercise. For household travel survey analysis of walking trip generation, the authors reported both overall performance and context-specific variation rather than relying on a single average estimate. The study design was appropriate for the target application but does not establish that the same relationships would hold under different operational or population conditions when interpreting results for household travel survey analysis of walking trip generation. In practical terms, the results are discussed in relation to the primary transport, health, behavioural or urban-management objective of the study, supporting the study's primary application involving household travel survey analysis of walking trip generation.

text: Urban and transport research increasingly combines sensing, geospatial data and machine learning to study a wide range of behaviours and environmental outcomes, creating a methodological challenge for studies of deep learning estimation of building height from aerial imagery. The investigation modelled associations relevant to deep learning estimation of building height from aerial imagery at the spatial and temporal scale required by that application. Accurate building height data support a range of urban analyses. This work trains a network to regress building height from high-resolution aerial imagery combined with shadow information, evaluated against airborne lidar-derived reference heights. Performance was assessed across building typologies and densities. Following data harmonisation, the predictors were combined with relevant demographic, operational or contextual covariates and evaluation focused on prediction error, association strength or operational performance. The analytical results were interpreted across alternative specifications and study subgroups to identify where performance or associations varied across contexts. Errors were largest for low-rise structures in dense blocks, and the derived height layer was released for the study region. Before modelling deep learning estimation of building height from aerial imagery, descriptive summaries were used to identify imbalance, missingness and implausible observations in the available data. Taken together, the results are discussed in relation to the primary transport, health, behavioural or urban-management objective of the study, with the principal contribution remaining the analysis of deep learning estimation of building height from aerial imagery.

text: Efficient allocation of cleansing resources requires knowledge of where waste accumulates. Many studies concerned with cities or mobility use technologies that also appear in pedestrian research, although the measured outcome may be different; the present study addressed this issue through street cleansing operations. The study modelled associations relevant to street cleansing operations while preserving the original outcome definition. Imagery collected from municipal service vehicles was processed with a detection model to identify litter, fly-tipping and overflowing bins along carriageways. Detections were aggregated by route and compared with existing complaint-driven scheduling. For the main analysis, the predictors were combined with relevant demographic, operational or contextual covariates while retaining the outcome definition used in the source application. The system enabled reallocation of cleansing rounds and reduced repeat complaints in the pilot district. The estimated associations were interpreted with attention to the variables contributing most strongly to the primary outcome to identify where performance or associations varied across contexts. Interpretation of street cleansing operations followed model evaluation so that feature importance did not substitute for predictive or statistical validity. Overall, the study demonstrates the usefulness of the selected data and analytical method for its target urban application, supporting the study's primary application involving street cleansing operations.

text: Background: Understanding whether neighbourhood form contributes to health requires combining individual outcomes with appropriately defined environmental exposures; the present study addressed this issue through association between green space proximity and mental health outcomes. Access to green space has been linked to psychological wellbeing. The research tested the performance of the proposed approach for association between green space proximity and mental health outcomes using domain-specific reference data. Methods: This cohort analysis linked residential addresses to green space proximity computed from land cover databases and examined associations with validated mental health instruments over follow-up. Models adjusted for individual and area-level confounders. In the modelling stage, the data sources were harmonised before estimation of the study's primary outcome while retaining the outcome definition used in the source application. Results: The evaluation metrics were interpreted across alternative specifications and study subgroups to determine whether the proposed approach improved on established methods. Proximity to green space was associated with modestly better outcomes, with associations stronger among lower-income participants. Conclusions: In practical terms, the study informs epidemiological interpretation of neighbourhood exposures and their association with individual health or behaviour, with the principal contribution remaining the analysis of association between green space proximity and mental health outcomes.

text: Computational models are widely used to explore urban design scenarios for which comprehensive field observations are unavailable, a concern directly relevant to simulation of evacuation flows in a transport terminal. The investigation tested simulation of evacuation flows in a transport terminal in relation to the study's primary outcome at the spatial and temporal scale required by that application. Emergency planning requires understanding of egress behaviour under congestion. A microscopic pedestrian simulation model was calibrated with published fundamental diagrams and applied to a terminal layout under several incident scenarios. Sensitivity analysis explored the influence of pre-movement time distributions and exit availability. For the main analysis, the principal explanatory variables were entered into the statistical or machine-learning model and performance was assessed against a simpler baseline. The evaluation metrics were compared with attention to the variables contributing most strongly to the primary outcome to support interpretation of the study's principal domain-specific outcome. Results identified bottleneck locations and informed proposed layout modifications; no field observation was conducted. Before modelling simulation of evacuation flows in a transport terminal, descriptive summaries were used to identify imbalance, missingness and implausible observations in the available data. The authors note that generalisation beyond the study setting may depend on differences in sampling, data availability and local operating conditions before generalising findings about simulation of evacuation flows in a transport terminal. For the target application, the findings are intended to support scenario evaluation and design optimisation before implementation or field validation, supporting the study's primary application involving simulation of evacuation flows in a transport terminal.

text: Not all shade is equally effective, since reflected and emitted radiation from surrounding surfaces continues to load pedestrians. Pedestrian heat exposure is highly sensitive to shade, surface materials, radiation and local air movement, variables that are not resolved by standard weather stations; the present study addressed this issue through ground-level radiometric measurement of shade quality along pedestrian arcades. The investigation tested whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for ground-level radiometric measurement of shade quality along pedestrian arcades at a resolution suitable for pedestrian-environment assessment. Net radiometers and globe thermometers were deployed at pedestrian height beneath arcades, tree canopies and fabric canopies along the same street. Mean radiant temperature was computed for each shading type across clear summer days. After preprocessing, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. Tree canopies outperformed built shading of equivalent geometric coverage, and the differential was attributed to lower surface temperatures of vegetated surfaces. The resulting measurements were contrasted in relation to observed differences in pedestrian use, comfort or accessibility where such data were available to assess whether the observed pattern was sufficiently stable for practical interpretation. To preserve the practical meaning of ground-level radiometric measurement of shade quality along pedestrian arcades, results were reported in the original measurement units as well as in any derived indicator. At network scale, the results support the use of pedestrian-scale thermal measurements when prioritising shade, material or route interventions under hot-weather conditions, while retaining the local detail needed for interpreting ground-level radiometric measurement of shade quality along pedestrian arcades.

text: Vertical discontinuities determine route feasibility for many pedestrians. Small geometric discontinuities in pedestrian infrastructure can determine whether a route is usable, yet they are rarely documented consistently across an urban network, which is especially important when considering handrails, steps and level changes along pedestrian routes with mobile range sensing. This work tested the feasibility of retaining the variables underlying handrails, steps and level changes along pedestrian routes with mobile range sensing as route-level evidence with attention to repeatability and measurement validity. Mobile range sensing captured pedestrian routes, and a processing chain identified steps, ramps, level changes and the presence of handrails, recording their dimensions. Field verification confirmed detection reliability. Once the observations had been screened, the measured variables were preserved separately before any summary indicator was calculated so that persistent spatial patterns could be distinguished from transient variation. A substantial share of level changes exceeding the accessible threshold lacked any handrail, and their spatial distribution was concentrated on connections between residential terraces and the main street network. The spatial outputs were compared across contrasting route types and local environmental contexts to assess whether the observed pattern was sufficiently stable for practical interpretation. Overall, the resulting measurements provide actionable evidence for identifying local accessibility barriers that are obscured by nominal infrastructure inventories, providing a practical basis for future work on handrails, steps and level changes along pedestrian routes with mobile range sensing.

text: This work examined a sensing-based workflow for crossing sight lines using street-level imagery and geometry reconstruction without relying solely on a pre-existing neighbourhood score under real-world conditions. Recent advances in computer vision make it possible to quantify pedestrian-scale features over large street networks without relying exclusively on manual audits, which is especially important when considering crossing sight lines using street-level imagery and geometry reconstruction. Visibility between pedestrians and drivers at crossings is a determinant of safety. Street-level imagery and reconstructed geometry were used to compute available sight distance from typical pedestrian waiting positions at crossings, accounting for parked vehicles, vegetation and street furniture detected in the same imagery. Computed sight distances were validated against on-site measurement. After preprocessing, sensor outputs were aggregated at route-segment level rather than neighbourhood level allowing adjacent route alternatives to be compared directly. The spatial outputs were examined across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to separate persistent environmental differences from short-term fluctuations. Obstruction by permitted parking reduced sight distance below recommended values at a large fraction of unsignalised crossings. A sensitivity analysis for crossing sight lines using street-level imagery and geometry reconstruction repeated the main comparison using only locations with complete observations across all measurement periods. From a pedestrian-planning perspective, the results illustrate how pedestrian-perspective imagery can provide scalable measurements of environmental qualities that are poorly captured by conventional plan-view datasets, with particular relevance to crossing sight lines using street-level imagery and geometry reconstruction.

text: Outdoor thermal conditions are a major determinant of whether walking remains comfortable and feasible during warm periods, which is especially important when considering sensing footway surface temperature and moisture to characterise slip and heat conditions. Surface state affects both slip risk and thermal comfort. The study examined whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for sensing footway surface temperature and moisture to characterise slip and heat conditions so that local conditions remained interpretable after aggregation. A pedestrian-borne rig combining infrared surface thermometry and a moisture sensor traversed footways across seasons, and readings were georeferenced and aggregated by segment and material. In the final processing stage, the cleaned observations were aligned with the locations at which pedestrians would encounter the condition so that short-distance variation remained visible. For sensing footway surface temperature and moisture to characterise slip and heat conditions, reference observations were kept separate from the main processing wherever possible so that agreement could be evaluated independently. The route-level indicators were examined across repeated measurement periods to assess temporal stability to assess whether the observed pattern was sufficiently stable for practical interpretation. Shaded stone surfaces retained moisture substantially longer after rainfall, and exposed asphalt reached surface temperatures that coincided with locations of reported discomfort in a parallel survey. At network scale, these observations show that thermal comfort is sufficiently localised to warrant direct inclusion in fine-grained walkability assessment, providing a practical basis for future work on sensing footway surface temperature and moisture to characterise slip and heat conditions.

text: Assessing a walking network requires information about the quality and operation of crossings rather than simply their location; the present study addressed this issue through visual attention to hazards during walking with mobile eye tracking. Whether pedestrians notice hazards depends on the visual environment. The study tested whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for visual attention to hazards during walking with mobile eye tracking while preserving variation between adjacent walking segments. Participants walked routes containing typical hazards such as raised slabs, bollards and cyclist crossings while wearing mobile eye-tracking glasses, with gaze mapped onto segmented imagery of the same locations. Fixation on hazards was related to visual clutter measured from the imagery. In the final processing stage, measurements were time-stamped and linked to individual walking segments to avoid masking local differences through area-wide averaging. The segment-level estimates were examined between neighbouring links with otherwise similar network characteristics to assess whether the observed pattern was sufficiently stable for practical interpretation. Detection of low-contrast hazards declined markedly in visually complex settings, with implications for hazard marking. The study was limited to a finite set of locations and seasons, so additional validation would be required before applying the same thresholds elsewhere in relation to visual attention to hazards during walking with mobile eye tracking. At network scale, the resulting measures can be incorporated into route-level accessibility and safety assessment rather than treating all mapped crossings as equivalent, while retaining the local detail needed for interpreting visual attention to hazards during walking with mobile eye tracking.

text: Pedestrian counts and movement patterns provide direct evidence of how walking environments are used over time, creating a methodological challenge for studies of footway counts using stereo cameras to evaluate a pedestrianisation scheme. Robust evaluation requires continuous measurement over an adequate period. The investigation assessed whether direct observations could provide sufficient spatial detail for footway counts using stereo cameras to evaluate a pedestrianisation scheme at a resolution suitable for pedestrian-environment assessment. Stereo cameras with automated detection recorded footway volumes and directional flows at treated and comparison streets for six months before and twelve months after a pedestrianisation scheme. Counts were validated against manual observation. For spatial analysis, measurements were time-stamped and linked to individual walking segments so that persistent spatial patterns could be distinguished from transient variation. A sensitivity analysis for footway counts using stereo cameras to evaluate a pedestrianisation scheme repeated the main comparison using only locations with complete observations across all measurement periods.
